lesson.title: When the Average Lies: Spotting a Biased Estimator
lesson.summary: A biased estimator is one whose sampling distribution is centered somewhere other than the true parameter, so it systematically overestimates or underestimates no matter how many times you sample.
lesson.body:
If an unbiased estimator is an archer whose shots are centered on the bullseye, a biased estimator is one whose shots are centered somewhere else entirely. Formally, the bias of an estimator equals the mean of its sampling distribution minus the true value of the parameter. When that difference is zero, the estimator is unbiased, as covered in the previous chapter. When it is not zero, the estimator is biased, and the sign and size of that difference tell you the direction and severity of the problem.

Bias is dangerous precisely because collecting more data from the same flawed procedure does not fix it. Repeating a biased sampling process a thousand times and averaging the results still converges to the wrong number, just with less noise around that wrong number. This is different from the kind of error caused by a small sample, which shrinks as sample size grows. A biased estimator has a design flaw, not a data shortage.

A classic example is using the sample maximum to estimate a population maximum. Consider a tiny population of four values: 1, 2, 3, and 4, so the true population maximum is 4. Take every possible sample of size two without replacement. There are six such samples: {1,2} with maximum 2, {1,3} with maximum 3, {1,4} with maximum 4, {2,3} with maximum 3, {2,4} with maximum 4, and {3,4} with maximum 4. Averaging these six sample maximums gives (2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 4) / 6 = 20 / 6, which is approximately 3.33. That average, 3.33, is less than the true population maximum of 4. The sample maximum is a biased estimator of the population maximum, and it is biased low: a sample can never contain a value larger than the population maximum, but it very often contains a value smaller than it, so the sampling distribution of the sample maximum is pulled below the true parameter.

This is also why introductory statistics courses divide by n minus 1, rather than n, when computing a sample variance to estimate a population variance. Dividing by n produces an estimator that is centered slightly below the true population variance on average, a small but genuine bias, and dividing by n minus 1 corrects it so the estimator is unbiased. You will not be asked to derive that correction here, but it is worth knowing that the choice of formula, not just the choice of data, can be the source of bias.

The takeaway for the rest of this unit is a standard to hold every new statistic to. When we introduce the sample proportion and the sample mean in the coming chapters, we will explicitly check where the mean of each one's sampling distribution falls. Both will turn out to be unbiased estimators of their respective parameters, which is one of the main reasons statisticians rely on them so heavily.
